title: Dale Wright Challenges of Zen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reports on Florence Caplow's Shuso ceremony at the Bay Area Everyday Zen Sangha, where Florence answers Nomon's question "Is this enough?" with "Yes. Right now, it is." Nomon then returns to Professor Dale Wright's address to Soto Zen priests in Oregon and lists the challenges Wright named: Zen's distance from politics and the environment, its dismissal of intellect, its tough-guy streak, and its limited attention to suffering. Nomon closes with poems by Hafiz and Rumi, and a discussion follows about whether practice itself is a form of service. Nomon answers with the sandwich question: can a small sangha also make sandwiches for the homeless?

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody.
Happy Halloween.
I'm not sure how you'd say it exactly, because it would be "Buenos los Días de Muerte."
Happy Day of the Dead.
I'm trying to figure out how to say that properly.
Happy All Saints Day tomorrow.
It seems like most little cultures have some kind of ritual or celebration, usually connected to the boundary between life and death, this time of year.
This year our weather and culture are well suited.
There's actually a ceremony in Zen.
Maybe next year we'll start to celebrate the Hungry Ghost.
I wanted to bring you a little report from the Bay Area Everyday Zen Sangha that I visited on Sunday, on a jet-setting Dharma journey.
One of the steps of training in this system is when there's a practice period.
Most of the sanghas in this lineage have a practice period once a year.
We'll have one in January, February, one in March this coming year.
The practice is to have one person be the sort of head student of the practice period.
There's a Japanese name, Shuso, which I think actually means "first seat," something like that.
The head student does some teaching, and the idea is that they're like the hub of the wheel: the sangha is the wheel and they're the hub.
There's a teacher out here, maybe starting to go moving, but the Shuso is the hub of the wheel.
At the end of the practice period you have a special ceremony.
Sometimes it's called the ceremony for the Shuso, sometimes it's called the Dharma inquiry ceremony.
They have a large practice period in the Bay Area, where Norman Fischer is the teacher.
Quite a few people are local, and local there means drive an hour and a half from Berkeley and stuff like that, so they have a big region that's local.
They also have many people participating remotely by listening to the talks online and having phone calls with the practice leader.
This is my teacher and the guiding figure of our sangha.
They just finished a practice period and ended on Sunday.
The head student, the Shuso, was Florence Caplow.
She's one of the founders of our sangha, a wonderful woman.
I went to be there for her ceremony, and it was really beautiful.
Florence clearly had really touched the hearts of everyone in the practice period, and there were many statements of appreciation.
Everyone asked a question of the head student in the ceremony, a Dharma question, and the head student's job was just to respond.
Not exactly to give an answer or give them counseling or something like that, but just to somehow meet them in that moment of the ceremony with some words or some gesture.
In the questions there was a lot of appreciation and a lot of love, and it was a very loving ceremony.
I don't think Zen is not loving, but it is.
I asked Florence, "Is this enough?
How would you answer that question, is this enough?"
And she said, "Yes.
Right now, it is."
I just wanted to mention that.
Our colleague and early member of the Red Cedar Zen Community, before it was even called that, completed a step in training and appears to have done a really wonderful job.
Now I want to return to a topic from a few weeks ago, when I was at another meeting, another Dharma trip, to Oregon this time.
There was a wonderful talk to this group of 90 Soto Zen priests from all over the country by a Buddhist scholar named Dale Wright, Professor Dale Wright.
He had the courage and audacity to tell us what was right about Zen and what the challenges of Zen are, which I thought was really great.
I gave a talk a couple of weeks ago listing some of the great strengths of Zen, according to Dale Wright.
I'll just highlight a few in case you weren't here.
I do have recordings of these; I'm just a little behind getting them on the website.
He felt Zen was a fairly unique and powerful spiritual tradition for a couple of different reasons.
He was quite a broad scholar of religion, knows many languages and has studied many religions.
So he's not narrowly a Buddhist scholar, I should say; he's a religious scholar.
He was impressed that Zen has a very strong moral and ethical dimension.
Zen practices deeply support positive internal qualities, mindfulness, concentration, awareness, and just help to create excellent human beings.
And practice itself is taken very seriously in the Zen tradition.
He said Zen is very good at just being down to earth, setting aside the otherworldliness of religion, is the way he described it.
He was impressed that Zen has no list of required beliefs.
I don't know if you've ever looked at a brochure, sometimes brochures from Christian groups, that say, "These are our beliefs, you can believe this and you're going to be happy here."
We don't have that.
It's a little bit awkward sometimes.
You're like, "What do you believe?"
He was impressed that Zen is sympathetic to science and modern understandings of the world.
Zen has a focus on freedom, it can be playful, and it has a strong aesthetic and literary tradition.
It also has a feeling of encouragement towards really deep engagement, that Zen has an idea of going beyond the master.
He said that's fairly unique; other religions don't have that so much.
So I mentioned that a couple of weeks ago.
Then he also listed six or seven challenges, weaknesses and challenges of Zen.
I want to mention what Dale Wright thinks our weaknesses and challenges are, so we can feel whether there's something we want to work on, or whether we agree with Professor Wright.
The first was this.
On the one hand, Zen explicitly talks about ethical conduct and morality.

On the other hand, there are many examples in the history of Zen, of Zen leaders and Zen institutions, feeling separate from political and moral reality, sort of above it all, which I suppose is not unusual for religion.

Zen can lean into a sense of the empty nature of all things, and then it doesn't really matter if there are wars or troubles; the temple can be beautiful and peaceful, surrounded by poverty and disaster.
He felt that was a bit of a problem, a kind of looseness from the moral and political sphere.
Another thing he was critical of is that sometimes Zen teachings seem to be intellectually dismissive: "Don't try to understand that.
This is beyond understanding."
Similar to the political challenge, there's a very similar strain with intellectualism, that Zen is somehow a special intellect beyond intellect, and this can be a form of control and manipulation.
That seems a little in contrast with his strength of Zen being down to earth, so these are tensions in both directions.
Another limitation or challenge of Zen, he felt, was that there is a great tension between the creation of extraordinary individuals and ordinary everyday life.
On the one hand, Zen seems to value the ordinariness of everyday life; just to hold a teacup in your hand is a deep Dharma, a powerful teaching.
And then we have these great and powerful archetypes of the Zen master, of enlightenment, of going beyond the ordinary.
So he felt Zen has a little work to do in merging the extraordinary and the ordinary more thoroughly.
Another limitation of Zen, he felt, is that Zen can be strong in a way that's rigid and unbending.
One of our great Zen ancestors, this character Bodhidharma, is presented as just unbelievably tough, so there's the tough-guy-ness of Zen, or this samurai sensibility of Zen.
He felt we're making progress in that, partly just because we have women teachers and leaders, and men and women practice together, which helps to soften this machismo of Zen.
And in Western Zen we're appreciating more Bodhisattvas and Zen symbols like Kuan Yin, of Avalokiteshvara, who's usually the female figure actually, and Jizo, who we have in the meeting room there.
We're appreciating more art types and images from the Buddhist tradition that are about caring, that are about nurturing, that are about love, and not just emphasizing wisdom.
Actually, this character Manjushri is the Bodhisattva of wisdom, and I was explaining to a couple of guys a couple of weeks ago that in a traditional Zen hall, well, you have lots of halls, right?
That's part of it.
But in the traditional Zen hall, you just have the Bodhisattva of wisdom in the middle, that's it.
So the traditional take on Zen meditation is just about wisdom.
Dale felt that was a bit of a problem, but something we're making good progress on, and he was proud of that: having a more nuanced view of wisdom and compassion working together.
This next one surprised me.
He said he feels Zen Buddhism is very weak on environmental awareness.
When he said that, it made me think of the Soto Zen Church, which is like the Catholic Church of our lineage, that we don't have too much connection to here.
For a while they had this green project.
I remember Robby Pellet was excited about this green project.
As far as I could tell, what the green project was, was sending all the temples green little tchotchkes.
Robby gave me, I think I still have it, this little green strap that could hold your cell phone around your wrist or something.
And he said, "Think green."
So that's what Dale was talking about.
On the one hand, Zen temples everywhere are beautiful and protect lands.

I remember he was saying that it's another version of this holding oneself separate: "I'm a Bodhisattva in a place of practice and I don't need to worry about environmental collapse or anything like that."
Another thing he felt Zen had a little bit of work to do on, and I'm not sure if I agree with him here, is that Zen practitioners could get better at directly attending to suffering.
We talk about suffering, we look at our inner suffering, we grow through the practice of awareness and transformation of suffering.

But he said that most other religions, and this probably is true, are much better at creating charities and sending people out into the world and having volunteers in hospitals and going into disasters.
Zen people are maintaining emptiness or something like that.
So that's an interesting question.
Can we, or should we, or is it even reasonable and possible for us as a community to directly attend to suffering?
His last suggestion was that we need to continue on with the project of reinventing what it is to have a truly American Zen Buddhism, or North American Zen Buddhism.
Ultimately, to really be meaningful and sustainable and real, it needs to become a truly American religion.
I have a list here, this must be what he mentioned: food, education, illness, etc.
I'm not sure what that list means anymore.
Basically, the theme of what he was saying is that Zen is a powerful practice of cultivating wisdom, and understanding, and extraordinary people, but in that process it can hold itself apart.
His challenge to us was a kind of radical inclusiveness: including suffering beings, including the environment, including the feminine, including innovation, including the whole world.
How that will actually play out in practice is a real question.
I'm not really sure.
But can Zen maintain all these wonderful qualities of creating powerfully sane, grounded, moral individuals working on their freedom, cultivating a deep aesthetic sensibility?
Can our little sanghas do all that, and also make sandwiches for the homeless?
Probably.
We also attend the environment.
So maybe it's looking at the ways in which we feel separate.
Here's a poem from a Sufi poet, Hafiz.
Maybe a little bit about this.
The title in the translation is "There could be holy fallout."
There could be holy fallout.
*We are often in battle, so often defending every side of the fort.
It may seem all alone.
Sit down, my dear.
Take a few breaths.
Think about a loyal friend.
Where is your music, your pet, a brush?
Surely one who has lasted as long as you knows some avenue or place inside that can give a sweet respite.*
*We are often in battle, so often defending every side of the fort.
It may seem all alone.
Sit down, my dear.
Take a few deep breaths.
Think about a loyal friend.
Where is your music, your pet, a brush?
Surely one who has lasted as long as you knows some avenue or place inside that can give a sweet respite.*
And here's a connective poem from Rumi.
Maybe this is Rumi's advice to Hafiz about how to actually do this.
"Two kinds of intelligence."
*Two kinds of intelligence.* Somehow this all feels connected to Dale Wright, but maybe not.
*There are two kinds of intelligence.
One acquired as a child in school, memorizes facts and concepts from books and from what the teacher says, collecting information from the traditional sciences as well as from the new sciences.
With such intelligence, you rise in the world.
You get ranked ahead or behind others in regard to your competence in retaining information.
You stroll with this intelligence in and out of the fields of knowledge, getting always more marks on your preserving tablets.
And there's another kind of tablet, one already completed and preserved inside you.
A spring overflowing in its spring box.
A freshness in the center of the chest.
This other intelligence does not turn yellow or stagnate.
It's fluid.
It doesn't move from outside to inside through the conduits of plumbing and learning.
This second knowing is a fountainhead from within you moving out.*
*Two kinds of intelligence.
One acquired as a child in school, memorizes facts and concepts from books and from what the teacher says, collecting information from the traditional sciences as well as from the new sciences.
With such intelligence, you rise in the world.
You get ranked ahead or behind others in regard to your competence in retaining information.
You stroll with this intelligence in and out of fields of knowledge, getting always more marks on your preserving tablets.
There's another kind of tablet though, one already completed and preserved inside you.
A spring overflowing in its spring box.
A freshness in the center of the chest.
This other intelligence does not turn yellow or stagnate.
It's fluid.
It doesn't move from outside to inside through conduits of plumbing and learning.
This second knowing is a fountainhead from within you moving out.*
So it seems like there's, in all these different ways of thinking and talking about religion or ourself or our suffering, somehow it gets into two categories, doesn't it?
This one who's beleaguered.
This one who can rest.
This one who's smart in a certain way, full of good information.
This one who trusts that which is already complete.
So this is kind of form and emptiness, right?
Again from our Heart Sutra that we chanted.
From the wisdom of moving back and forth, fluidly, in a way that helps ourselves and others, is what they mean by Prajnaparamita in that chant.
So that's my little semi-coherent talk for this evening.
My plan starting next week is to go through the seven factors of enlightenment.
So I may go a little more.
I'm kind of feeling my way into how to use a short talk period, so I've been experimenting a little bit.
Last week we took a little break and learned from Martin Batchelor.
He's quite a wonderful person.
I hope you got a sense of her a little bit from that recording.
So what do you think?
Comments?
Questions?
Poems?
Cool, more minutes.
**Participant:** Well, I was thinking, it seems like regular practice helps us just be more compassionate in the world.
I think it addressed suffering in a more direct, helpful way than without practice.
I don't completely agree with...

I mean, you can certainly volunteer in hospitals and do things like that, but just to be able to, in your family, and knowing people you know in your life, should be a lot more compassionate and giving in the little ways that arise.
I think that's...
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, I agree with you.
I'm not sure if I drew a tail there either.
I mean, he might be sort of making an organizational critique of what happens in places in Japan and America.
But what I think about that, too, is if we're sort of grounded in emptiness and practice, then we can help in a much more sustainable way.
You know, it's interesting.
I did a class for a group of helping professionals, a mindfulness class for a group of helping professionals.
Mostly it was therapists and nurses and naturopaths.
And they talked a lot about the way, after they've worked with the client, it's really suffering how they really end up, and then they have all these ways to try to sort of clear that again.
And I didn't very successfully help them with this, but I'm musing about how to sort of express that there's a way that our Dharma practice...
Don't you think, John?

The way our Dharma practice allows us to be with suffering without that sort of stickiness and that sort of absorbing of that toxicity, where we can really help and then move on and help the next person and take care of ourselves.
**Participant:** It seems like it does help, but maybe it's just a little nudge, like sometimes maybe a little nudge off the cushion to put this into action.
I see that the action is facing one's own demons.
Right.
Which is a huge task for everybody, for each of us.
And the practice allows us to do that and promote that.
And it's kind of like we gather together to do that for the world.
Because in this particularly contemporary life, it's so busy running around, it's scattered, it's distracted, and unable to go around.
Right.
It seems like also the more we know our own demons, the easier it is for us to be sympathetic and patient with others.
But it is kind of like a full-time job.
Yeah, right, right.
We can't go out and work for them.
When does Dale think we're going to have time for all this?
It is terribly absorbing.
It is, yeah.
I don't think it means ourselves.
I think it means us something that's really hard to do.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Well, it's a different kind of service.
If you make a sandwich with somebody, it's different than to be able to really hear somebody's pain and be still with it and be relaxed with it, so that they can really do something differently.
I think it's a very important value.
And I think the other thing we know from our practice, too, is there are many different ways of getting somebody a sandwich.
Some of which are harmful.
Yeah.
Some of which are actually harmful.
**Participant:** I think about how hard it is to really be or try to be helpful and decrease someone else's suffering if you're not able to decrease your own in some way.
How attentive can you actually be to the other person's suffering, to the other person's light and difficulties, if somehow you're able to deal with your own.
There's that thing about contagion and how you pick up other people's troubles when you work with them.
But there's that other thing about being really clear and clean yourself before you start.
My experience with myself is the less clear I am, the more guarded I am of myself.
And I'm not able to be fully present with that other person anymore.
And so on.
From what necessarily to what's in tries to do.
I don't know how to call and make some sort of exact balance in picking sandwiches' direction.
It's an upright direction.
There probably is one.
But that's just my own experience.
The more I'm clear, the more I can actually deal with the other person without guarding myself.
Not being run by the demons that you were talking about.
And being on the other side of that when you're trying to get help from somebody who's not real clear.
I mean, they know they want to help but they haven't dealt with themselves.
So they're kind of doing it rote.
But that can be very painful on the inside.
It's not genuine.
And yet you know this person is trying, and so then you wonder, am I not getting it?
But you know, I can feel in my gut that they don't have it.
And that can be really confusing.
I don't know.
I really...
That was actually the one that...
Well, there were a couple of challenges that really made for me.
And that was actually one of them.
And I don't feel it as acutely now.
But it's definitely something that's come to my mind several times in this community and with this practice.
Is that same feeling of our...
Yeah, we're attending to ourselves.
But are we attending to the larger picture?
And I think to me it's just the fact that it is so internal.
So it's like each one of us could be...
I mean, we all have our own personal suffering.
But they're kept private within the context of the practice.
And I really wonder at times what would it be like to practice hearing people's stories?
And to be able to have a practice that, instead of reinforcing the solitariness so much, reinforced the fact that we all have similar suffering.
And to really be able to...
Like, I think there's a piece of kind of letting go of the individuality of our own sufferings that you can only really do if you know about other people's.
I mean, I know I definitely find this with a lot of my girlfriends who we're going through similar things.
And it's like there's that knowing of I'm not alone in this.

We've all got a piece of some of these experiences that I think does then make a real impact in how you respond in the world and whether you do keep yourself aloof or whether you're really called to take action.
And I think it really has to do with do we define ourselves as individuals or do we define ourselves as part of a group of people who have whatever similarities those may be.
And there are a lot of different experiences that can lead to that sense of solidarity.
But I really think that, to me, that's a big piece of support.
I don't know, just what's important and what brings forth that engagement with the world is the solidarity with other people who are suffering in similar ways as you've suffered.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** Yeah, for sure.
Yeah, there's a lot of...
I'm in touch with all these funny branches of scientific research in the Dharma, right?
So there's knowledge, research on compassion, the scientific studies of compassion.
I'm not kidding.
And one of the precursors, one of the definitions of compassion, the precursors for compassion, is what they call the sense of shared humanity, the feeling of shared humanity.
That the person has to feel some connection.
And it's interesting, I mean, it does seem like that can have an element of shared stories, but it can also have an element of shared experience without stories too, which is also interesting.
That's been fun for me doing this.
Lately I've done a few retreats for these mindfulness classes and that feeling has come up.
People saying, "I don't really know you people that well, but boy, I feel so close to you and so connected just from doing practice together."
So I think both form and emptiness have a role there for sure.
Thank you for mentioning that, Georgia.
Okay, well that's, thank you for a nice discussion, yeah.
It's good to bring these things up and use them.
So thank you, Dr.
Wright, for criticizing us so much so we can see ourselves.
